system_description.narrative_title: A Tightly Coupled Global Order: Markets, Energy, and Geopolitics in Feedback
system_description.narrative_summary: The global order is an open, tightly coupled system in which a synchronized shock to energy supplies, high government debt and a renewed bond-market rout are amplifying political and security risks. Geopolitical flashpoints—from the Middle East and Iran-related shipping and force deployments to Russia’s strikes in Ukraine and US–China trade-tech frictions—are feeding commodity and risk premia, which in turn drive financial stress, policy reactions and cross-border interventions. Domestic politics (notably US policy ahead of midterms and fiscal strains in Europe) are shaping outward-facing tools—export controls, sanctions, reserve releases and military deployments—creating nonlinear feedbacks across markets, supply chains and alliance politics.
system_description.scope: States, alliances and regional security theatres; global financial markets (sovereign and corporate bond markets, central banks); energy and commodity flows and stockpiles; multinational supply chains and trade controls; major corporations, tech platforms and investors; military deployments and security incidents; multilateral institutions and crisis-response mechanisms.
system_description.super_system: The planetary socio-economic-political system (globalized civilization: economic, ecological and technological networks across the Anthropocene).

variables.name: Global bond market stress
variables.description: US, European and Asian central banks, large institutional investors and sovereign borrowers are confronting a sustained sell‑off and rising long-term yields that are re-pricing fiscal risks and the global monetary-policy outlook.

variables.name: Middle East military escalation
variables.description: Iran, regional proxies, Israel and the United States are locked in a cycle of strikes, maritime interdictions and military deployments that is intensifying regional instability and testing deterrence relationships.

variables.name: Russia–Ukraine high-intensity war
variables.description: Russia and Ukraine, supported respectively by Western military supply chains and sanctions coalitions, remain engaged in sustained high‑intensity combat and strategic strikes that are degrading infrastructure and reshaping European defence commitments and NATO posture.

variables.name: US–China strategic competition
variables.description: The United States and China are contesting technological, economic and military influence—via export controls, investment frictions and increased activity around Taiwan and the South China Sea—driving supply‑chain realignments and alliance hedging across the Indo‑Pacific.

variables.name: Global fuel and refining shock
variables.description: Producers, refiners and consuming states are grappling with a refining and distribution crunch—seen in diesel shortages, export curbs, high freight costs and coordinated reserve releases—that is elevating fuel prices and prompting emergency policy coordination.
